title: A passed pawn: push, support or hold back?
outcomes: Decides, in a position with a passed pawn, whether the best plan is to push it, support it or play elsewhere
Predicts how moving the White king closer to or further from the pawn changes win and draw in a pawn ending
Names, on paper, the enemy piece or king that the passed pawn ties down (unchecked by the app)

steps.text: This lesson builds on **Passed pawns: blockade early, if you can arrive in time**. A passed pawn gives you three choices: **push** it, **support** it (with the king or a piece), or **hold back** and improve something else. The pawn is an asset, not a duty. First find it, then ask what stands in front of it and who watches its path.

**Push** when the push gains something concrete and the squares ahead are not held by enemy pieces. **Support** when the pawn cannot go alone; in an ending the king is the best helper. **Hold back** when the push loses the pawn or lets the enemy trade it off. *Rule of thumb:* ask what each option does before you touch the pawn.

steps.title: Supporting with the king
steps.prompt: Only the White king differs. Is the second position still a win? Predict, then check.

steps.text: A passed pawn also works without moving: the other side often has to keep a piece or the king ready to stop it, so one defender may be tied to the pawn. When you look at a passed pawn, name that piece. The board cannot check this for you, so write it down yourself.

steps.prompt: Look back at the first position of this lesson, with the Black pawn on c4. Name the White piece that has to watch the pawn, or say there was none. Then say whether the Black king's place changed what White had to do.
